In respirometry trials conducted at a stable environmental temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the resting metabolic rate of adult Dryophytes cinereus was measured and found to be 0.0113 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0113 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value represents the maximum basal metabolic rate for the species and aligns with energetics expected for a small-bodied hylid frog, consistent with values reported for other members of the Hylidae family of similar mass. The relatively low oxygen consumption reflects the modest daily energetic costs of tissue upkeep in an ambush predator that spends much of its time perched motionless on vegetation. The experimental animals were collected from populations in the southeastern United States and were acclimated to laboratory conditions for several weeks prior to measurement. All trials were performed on post-absorptive individuals during their inactive photophase to ensure true basal conditions were obtained.

The wet weight at birth, inferred from the diameter of the fertilised ovum, is remarkably small at 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. This figure is derived from a yolk-laden egg measuring approximately 2 mm in diameter, and the minuscule mass of the newly emerged aquatic larva starkly contrasts with the much larger adult body size. Newly hatched tadpoles are endotrophic for a brief period, subsisting entirely on remaining yolk reserves before they commence first exogenous feeding. At a controlled water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the age at birth, or time to eclosion from the gelatinous egg mass, was recorded as 10 days [ab = 10 days]. This hatching duration falls within the published range of 4 to 14 days observed in natural ponds, where thermal variability can accelerate or delay embryonic development. The small initial mass imposes constraints on early larval survival, as newly emerged individuals are vulnerable to both predation and desiccation of their aquatic habitat.

Female American green tree frogs eventually attain a maximum adult body mass of 5.1 grams [Wwi = 5.1 grams], making them noticeably larger than conspecific males. This ultimate wet weight for females reflects the substantial energetic investment required for gamete production and the physical accommodation of a large clutch volume. The developmental journey from a 0.0042 gram hatchling to a fully grown adult involves a multi-thousand-fold increase in mass, driven by an extended period of larval and juvenile feeding on arthropod prey. At the standard reference temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis was observed to be 34 days . During this larval period, the exogenously feeding tadpole undergoes significant morphological transformation, including limb bud development and tail resorption, culminating in the terrestrial transition of a froglet. This relatively rapid larval phase is typical for a species that breeds in ephemeral water bodies that may dry quickly.

Under the same controlled thermal conditions of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum lifespan for this species was determined to be approximately 2263 days [am = approximately 2263 days]. This longevity figure, derived from long-term captive records and mark-recapture field studies, underscores the relatively rapid life-history pace of a small anuran that faces high predation pressure. Following metamorphosis, the terrestrial juvenile enters a period of rapid growth and sexual maturation. The time since metamorphosis at puberty for females has been documented at 730 days [tp = 730 days] at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This two-year delay before gonadal maturation allows the frog to accumulate sufficient body size and lipid stores to support the energetic demands of egg production. Individuals that reach this threshold successfully then transition into reproductively active adults capable of participating in the annual breeding choruses that characterize the species' reproductive ecology.

The maximum daily reproduction rate for this species is best understood through the separate components of fecundity and spawning frequency. Gravid females produce an average of 3.35 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3.35 eggs per clutch], a modest number reflecting the species' small body size relative to other hylids. Each female typically produces one clutch per day [F_R_i = one clutch per day] during the peak of the breeding season at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], resulting in a substantial total reproductive output over the course of a summer. This pattern of continuous, low-volume egg deposition contrasts with the single, large clutch strategy seen in many explosive-breeding anurans. The cumulative annual reproductive effort, when sustained over the female's adult lifespan, represents a significant allocation of resources toward offspring production, a necessary trade-off given the high mortality rates faced by both aquatic eggs and terrestrial juveniles in the species typically active environment.
